## Background

The data for this hands-on session comes from a published RNA-seq experiment where airway smooth muscle cells (ASMs) were treated with dexamethasone (dex), a synthetic glucocorticoid steroid with anti-inflammatory effects (Himes et al. 2014).

```{r}
#BiocManager::install("DESeq2")

library(BiocGenerics)
library(DESeq2)
```


## Data Import

```{r}
counts <- read.csv("airway_scaledcounts.csv", row.names=1)
metadata <- read.csv("airway_metadata.csv")
```

> Q1. How many genes are in this dataset? 

```{r}
nrow(counts)
```

> Q2. How many total samples do we have and of those, how many ‘control’ cell lines do we have? 

```{r}
nrow(metadata)

#two ways to answer the controls part of this question
count(metadata$dex == "control")
table(metadata$dex)
```

There are a total of 8 samples, 4 of which are controls.


## Analysis

Lets just take out control samples and put theem in a table and then the same for treated. `Data.frames` !! 

```{r}
control.inds <- metadata$dex == "control"
control.counts <- counts[, control.inds]
dim(control.counts)

treated.inds <- metadata$dex == "treated"
treated.counts <- counts[, treated.inds]
dim(treated.counts)
```

```{r}
control.mean <- rowMeans(control.counts)
treated.mean <- rowMeans(treated.counts)

meancounts <- data.frame(control.mean, treated.mean)
head(meancounts)
```

>Q3. How would you make the above code in either approach more robust? Is there a function that could help here? 

Using `rowMeans()` is better than using something like `rowSums()/4` because then you're not hard ocdin how many rows there are incase there are more rows in a different data set. 

>Q4. Follow the same procedure for the treated samples (i.e. calculate the mean per gene across drug treated samples and assign to a labeled vector called treated.mean)

Done, see above.

> Q5 (a). Create a scatter plot showing the mean of the treated samples against the mean of the control samples.

```{r}
plot(meancounts)
```

>Q5(b) and Q6. You could also use the ggplot2 package to make this figure producing the plot below. Try plotting both axes on a log scale.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(meancounts, aes(control.mean, treated.mean)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

We often use the concept of "fold-change" this is just the log fraction of treated over control.

```{r}
20/20
log2(20/20)

40/20
log2(40/20)

20/40
log2(20/40)
```

```{r}
meancounts$log2fc <- log2(meancounts$treated.mean/meancounts$control.mean)

head(meancounts)
```

```{r}
#zero.vals <- which(meancounts[,1:2]==0, arr.ind=TRUE)

#to.rm <- unique(zero.vals[,1])
#counts <- meancounts[-to.rm,]
#head(counts)
```

> Q7. What is the purpose of the `arr.ind` argument in the `which()` function call above? Why would we then take the first column of the output and need to call the `unique()` function?

The `arr.ind` argument makes `which()` to give us the table info for the genes that it is `TRUE` for. The `unique()` would makes sure that we don't call anything twice.


Now, the NaN is returned when you divide by zero and try to take the log. The -Inf is returned when you try to take the log of zero. It turns out that there are a lot of genes with zero expression. Let’s filter our data to remove these genes.

```{r}
to.keep <- rowSums(meancounts[,1:2]) > 10
mycounts <- meancounts[to.keep,]
```

>Q8. How many genes are left? How many are upregulated

```{r}
nrow(mycounts)
sum(mycounts$log2fc >= 2)
```

>Q9. How many down regulated genes we have at the greater than 2 fc level? 

```{r}
sum(mycounts$log2fc <= -2)
```

>Q10. Do you trust these results? Why or why not?

Not yet, we haven't done any statistical analysis! 


## DESeq analysis

Let's put some stats behind these numbers.

```{r, message=F}
library(DESeq2)
```

Must supply 3 things in a very soecific data structure:

- countData (our counts)

- colData(our metadata)

- design(the setup of our experiment)

```{r}
#dds (deseq data set) is what its called in all the manuals
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts,
                              colData = metadata,
                              design = ~dex)
```

```{r}
dds <- DESeq(dds)

res <- results(dds)
head(res)
```

## Save our results

```{r}
write.csv(res, file="my_DESeq_results.csv")
```

## Summary results figure

A common summary figure is a volcano plot which combines log2 fold changes and adjusted p-values. 

```{r}
ggplot(res, aes(log2FoldChange, -log(padj))) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(+2,-2), col="magenta") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log(0.05), col="magenta")
```

Let's add color to be less boring.

```{r}
my.cols <- rep("gray", nrow(res))
my.cols[res$log2FoldChange>=2] <- "pink"
my.cols[res$log2FoldChange<=-2] <- "lightblue"
my.cols[res$padj>0.05] <- "grey"

ggplot(res, aes(log2FoldChange, -log(padj))) +
    geom_point(col=my.cols) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(+2,-2), col="magenta") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log(0.05), col="magenta")
```


## Adding annotation data

```{r, message=F, warning=F}
BiocManager::install("AnnotationDbi")
BiocManager::install("org.Hs.eg.db")

library("AnnotationDbi")
library("org.Hs.eg.db")
```

```{r}
columns(org.Hs.eg.db)
```

```{r}
res$symbol <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                     keys=row.names(res), # Our gene names
                     keytype="ENSEMBL",        # The format of our gene names
                     column="SYMBOL",          # The new format we want to add
                     multiVals="first")

head(res)
```


> Q11. Run the mapIds() function two more times to add the Entrez ID and UniProt accession and GENENAME as new columns called res$entrez, res$uniprot and res$genename

```{r}
res$entrez <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                     keys=row.names(res),
                     column="ENTREZID",
                     keytype="ENSEMBL",
                     multiVals="first")

res$uniprot <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                     keys=row.names(res),
                     column="UNIPROT",
                     keytype="ENSEMBL",
                     multiVals="first")

res$genename <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
                     keys=row.names(res),
                     column="GENENAME",
                     keytype="ENSEMBL",
                     multiVals="first")

head(res)
```

Let's organize by p-value:

```{r}
ord <- order(res$padj)
head(res[ord,])

write.csv(res[ord,], "deseq_results.csv")
```
